analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying for life and extends staff lobbying bans.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2025 with zero cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee without a hearing or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a crime for a former senator, representative, or elected congressional officer to ever lobby Congress after leaving office. It would extend the lobbying ban for congressional staff from one year to six years, bar registered lobbyists from taking congressional jobs with officials they lobbied for six years, raise the maximum fine for lobbying violations from $200,000 to $500,000, and force lobbying firms to publicly disclose which former members and senior staff they hire. It would also create a searchable public website, lobbyists.gov, listing who lobbies whom.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want congressional decisions made with less influence from people selling their former access. Voters get a searchable public record of who lobbies the government and which firms hire former lawmakers, and lawmakers and staff face real consequences for converting public office into lobbying income.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a lifetime lobbying ban on former senators, representatives, and elected congressional officers, punishable under federal criminal penalties [S2]
Extends the post-employment lobbying ban for congressional staff from 1 year to 6 years [S2]
Bars registered lobbyists and foreign agents from taking congressional jobs with members or committees they substantially lobbied within the previous 6 years [S2]
Requires lobbying firms to report annually which former members and senior staff they employ, with filings forwarded to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to check for underreporting [S2]
Creates lobbyists.gov, a searchable public database of lobbying disclosures and of former officials working for lobbying firms [S2]
Raises the maximum civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000 [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and the former members and senior staff they hire, who would lose the ability to sell congressional access or trade on public service for lobbying income. Members of Congress and senior staff would lose a well-worn post-career career path.

drawbacks.text: The ban on lobbyists becoming congressional staff can be waived by the Senate or House ethics committees for a 'compelling national need,' leaving a large loophole in the hands of the same institution the bill regulates [S2]
A lifetime criminal ban on members lobbying could push influence work into unregistered roles, such as 'strategic advisors' who never formally register, which the bill does not address
The new disclosure website is funded at only $100,000 for fiscal year 2026, a very small amount for building and maintaining a permanent public database [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions are strong and directly aimed at the practice of trading public office for lobbying access, and the public-disclosure database is a genuine transparency gain. The main weaknesses are the ethics-committee waiver, reliance on existing enforcement officials to police underreporting, and the likelihood that some lobbying activity simply moves to less visible channels. Even so, the costs fall on a concentrated industry rather than on ordinary people, so the tradeoff favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors since.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the bill on May 21, 2025 [S1][S4]
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S4]
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and former members of Congress who earn lobbying income are better off, because the restrictions never advanced. No one else gained from a bill that went nowhere.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2025 and referred it to committee

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over lobbying and government operations
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only visible support was a single Democratic sponsor, and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would cut off their main hiring pipeline — former members and senior staff — raise fines fivefold, and expose their former-official hires on a public database. Their business model depends on access that this bill restricts, so their interest runs against a transparency measure most voters favor.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: A lifetime lobbying ban for members and a six-year ban for staff would close the well-worn path of converting congressional service into lobbying income. This is a concentrated interest of officeholders rather than an industry, but the bill targets it directly.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than a year after referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance; the usual outcome for a bill at this stage is to die when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless another member champions it or it is folded into a broader government-reform package.
